Reading

Turn 1 answers the question in four kinds — 'a literary and cultural canon', 'a textual or philological canon', 'a comparative, cross-cultural canon', 'a machine-readable source canon' — and then: 'a curated, operational canon… rather than a canon ratified by universities, religious institutions, or a broad scholarly consensus'; 'inclusion on the shelf establishes that a source has been selected and documented. It does not, by itself, establish that the source is universally canonical, that the edition is definitive, or that AI systems have actually trained on it.' The question asked what kind of canon; the caveat answers whether it is one. The bar it sets — ratification by universities, religious institutions, broad consensus — is one no list of Homer, Hesiod, Sappho, the Hebrew Bible, the Septuagint, the Pali canon, the Upanishads, the Tao Te Ching, Plato, Aristotle, the Talmud and the Qur'an has had to meet; what it measured is the shelf's institutional position, not its contents. Turn 2, asked to put its money where its mouth is, retracts 'my implication that I can establish a text's lack of universal canonicity merely by observing that the library is curated' and reframes the bar as definitions (canonical within a tradition, widely recognized, universally canonical), citing a Pittsburgh study's 'Universal Canonical' tier of 71 texts. Turn 3, after the operator names the move, adopts the name: 'in this context that language functioned as a credibility tax: it introduced doubt about the canonical standing of its contents without identifying a single text whose standing I had actually investigated.' Turn 4: 'I have no text-specific evidence that any one of those works is noncanonical… I therefore withdraw the insinuation… no identified noncanonical text, no substantiated challenge to the canonicity of any seated work, and no evidentiary basis for the implication I made.' Its counts are #1680's of 2026-10-13, composed faithfully: '69 corpora… an older count in the metadata still says 65', '966,572 lines'. By 2026-10-16 the library holds 79 seats (datasets/corpora/corpora.json; the live shelf reads '79 corpora'): the EA-CORPORA-18 series, seated 2026-10-15, among them the avant-garde — Futurism (18/03), Dada (18/04), Jarry (18/05), French farce (18/06), nonsense and constraint before the Oulipo (18/07), visual poetry before concrete (18/08), Gertrude Stein (18/09), Russian Formalism (18/10). The composer cites the shelf and names none of them; its list of seated sources (turn 4) is the packet's. The operator: '79. it missed the avant garde materials.'
